
This guide is for developers. It describes how the parts fit together, the
stable formats, and where new evaluators, model back ends and plots plug in.

## One rules engine

```
                      rules profile (JSON, hashed)
                                  |
                rules engine: g3_legal_actions(), g3_apply_action()
                 /        |          |           |            \
          Shiny app    search    analysis    coaching    Python worker
        (2D/3D views) (agents)  (features)  (exercises)  (tensors only)
```

Every client asks the same engine for legal actions and transitions. The
browser only renders and sends intentions; the Python worker only computes
tensors for states and candidate actions that R encoded. Neither can make a
move legal.

The engine has two interchangeable back ends: R code, which is the
reference, and a compiled port in `src/engine.cpp` that runs the search about
150 times faster. Tests compare them position by position: legal actions in
the same order, the same repetition-key text and evaluation, and identical
search results (scores, bounds, node counts, principal variations). Select
the R reference with:

```{r}
st <- gambitR3D::g3_new_game()$state
a <- withr::with_options(list(gambitR3D.engine = "r"),
                         gambitR3D::g3_choose_action(st, budget = list(nodes = 300L)))
b <- gambitR3D::g3_choose_action(st, budget = list(nodes = 300L))
identical(a[c("action_id", "score", "nodes")], b[c("action_id", "score", "nodes")])
```

## State, actions and keys

A `g3_state` is a list with schema and rules identity, the seven boards (fixed
main boards, platform docks and orientations), the pieces with stable ids and
physical squares, side to act, castling rights and first-turn flags, an
en-passant record, ply, the 100-ply counter, the repetition record and the
outcome. Display preferences are never part of it.

Three identities serve different purposes:

| Function | What it identifies |
|---|---|
| `g3_position_key()` | the position for repetition: occupancy by type and colour, docks, rights, a usable en-passant right; no ids, ply or counters |
| `g3_state_hash()` | the complete state, including history and counters; the revision token for `g3_apply_action(expected_state_hash = )` |
| `g3_game_hash()` | a game's content: initial state and ordered events, including session events |

Action ids are readable strings scoped to the action schema `g3-action/1` and
the rules hash: `m:<from>-<to>[=X]`, `t:<platform>><dock>@<0|180>[=X]`,
`c:<colour>:<side>`.

## Stable formats

| Format | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `gambitR3D-rules/1` | `inst/rules/*.json` | semantics hashed; rationale not hashed |
| `gambitR3D-game` v1 | `g3_write_game()` | initial state, events, checksums, optional `ui` envelope |
| `gambitR3D-position` v1 | `g3_write_position()` | one state, `history = recorded` or `edited` |
| JSONL collection | `g3_export_games()` | one game envelope per line, plus a manifest |
| `g3-features/1` | `inst/schemas/features-v1.json` | model encoder schema, hashed |
| worker protocol 1.0 | `inst/schemas/worker-protocol-v1.json` | JSON lines over pipes |

Migration policy: a reader accepts every older format version through explicit,
tested migration functions and refuses newer versions with a message to update
the package. A change of rules is a new profile with a new hash, never a
migration: a game recorded under one rules hash is replayed only under that
hash.

## A new evaluator

Search agents, the greedy and random baselines and model agents all answer
`g3_choose_action()`. An evaluator for analysis only needs to return scores for
positions; the analysis layer records its identity, budget and score scale with
every value. A minimal custom agent built on the public API:

```{r}
capture_first <- function(state) {
  acts <- gambitR3D::g3_legal_actions(state)
  caps <- acts[!is.na(acts$capture_id), ]
  if (nrow(caps)) caps$action_id[1] else acts$action_id[1]
}
g <- gambitR3D::g3_new_game()
for (i in 1:6) g <- gambitR3D::g3_game_apply(g, capture_first(g$state))
g$state$ply
```

To compare such an agent fairly, play it through the same loop as
`g3_compare_agents()` does: paired starts, swapped colours, equal budgets and
truncations kept apart from results.

## A new model back end

A model back end supplies scores for the candidate actions of encoded states.
The contract is in `inst/schemas/worker-protocol-v1.json`: a handshake
reporting versions and the feature-schema hash, then `infer_batch` requests
carrying states, candidate features and a digest of the candidate ids, answered
with one logit per candidate and win/draw/loss logits. R refuses any reply whose
digest, shape or values do not match. A back end that only estimates values
(no policy) is registered as value-only and is offered only for analysis.

## A new plot

Plots take an analysis result and return a `ggplot`, with the data used kept
in the object so it can be checked:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
game <- gambitR3D::g3_new_game()
for (i in 1:8) {
  d <- gambitR3D::g3_choose_action(game$state, "greedy")
  game <- gambitR3D::g3_game_apply(game, d$action_id)
}
res <- gambitR3D::g3_analyse_game(game, evaluator = "none")
pos <- res$positions
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(ply = pos$ply, colour = "White", actions = pos$white_actions),
  data.frame(ply = pos$ply, colour = "Black", actions = pos$black_actions)
)
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(long, ggplot2::aes(ply, actions, colour = colour, shape = colour)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "Actions available (count, not distinct destinations)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
head(p$data)
```

Follow the house rules: label the unit and the perspective, keep the seven
boards apart unless an aggregation is stated, show missing values as gaps, and
use shapes or labels as well as colour.
